newsitem.title: UK: Drugs give AIDS patients new hope for life.
newsitem.headline: Drugs give AIDS patients new hope for life.

text.p: When Richard Eastman first smelled the drugs he was going to take, he was reminded of a pile of dirty socks. He feared the strong drugs could make him even sicker, but also felt he had no choice.
Eastman had advanced AIDS. He had contracted pneumonia, lost 30 pounds (14 kg) and his immune system was almost non-existent.
"I got so sick at one point that I thought I was going to die," Eastman, 43, told reporters at an AIDS conference.
Laid off from his job costuming film stars in Hollywood, he was living on social security with plenty of time on his hands to watch his weight drop and his immune system falter.
But doctors enrolled him in an experimental programme to test a new approach to treating AIDS, one using a triple combination of strong drugs to suppress the virus.
He was given an early version of Abbott Laboratories' protease inhibitor ritonavir (Norvir) along with the "standard" AIDS drug AZT and a similar drug.
According to Eastman, a miracle occurred. He gained weight and there were indications his immune system was strengthening. "I had some hope."

Like many AIDS patients, he is fluent in the language of T-cells and viral load. T-cells are immune system cells destroyed by HIV infection and a count of them indicates how badly the disease is progressing. Viral load measures how much virus is in the blood.
"At that time the drug was in liquid form," Eastman, a pale but energetic-looking man, said. "The drug tasted something similar to rotten socks and I had to take it two times a day."

Later, Abbott developed a tablet form and all the 1,000 patients in the trial were given ritonavir, even those who had been taking placebo doses containing no drug. Eastman immediately started getting better.
"In a matter of two weeks...this is all documented...my T-cells had raised to 80. This is a miracle."
It is, however, unclear what long term effect the combination treatment will have on HIV-infected people.

Eastman hopes he may be able to return to work one day. Speaking with the fervour of an evangelist, he praises the drugs and urges governments around the world to make the triple combination therapy available to everyone.
Angel Menendez of Barcelona, who developed AIDS in 1990, said his combination treatment had saved Spain's state-run healthcare system money.
"As soon as I heard protease inhibitors had been approved by the FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration), I was in the United States," he said.
He bought his own drugs, and the results were immediate.
"Last year I was very expensive for my government," he said. He was in hospital for six weeks with various infections -- all of his treatment paid for by the state.

But this year, he said, he had not been in the hospital at all. Doctors at the Third International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection have been presenting evidence on the cost- effectiveness of HIV combination therapy.
They say it will be cheaper for hospitals to treat AIDS patients with the drugs than to treat them for the diseases they get if they don't take the drugs.
Some early studies indicate a 50 percent reduction in hospitalisation and death if patients get the cocktails.
Kate Simpson of the University of North Carolina said she and fellow researchers reckoned that Spain, for example, could save $4,000 per patient per year by using combination therapy.
